## Methods

The proposed WTFTP+ framework
In the flight process, the overall motion trends of the aircraft are typically determined by historical transition patterns, flight plans, and real-time ATC instructions. To be specific, for a certain route, the longitude and latitude always evolve along the heading between two consecutive waypoints, indicating that the planned route (in the flight plans) can imply the overall flight trend. At the same time, local variations are introduced by weather conditions, aircraft performance parameters, and pilot-specific operations. In other words, a flight trajectory can be regarded as a combination of global trends and local details. While different flights in similar scenarios may follow similar overall trends, their local motion details often vary significantly, which limits the prediction accuracy of the conventional FTP approaches. Fortunately, the wavelet transform provides an intuitive solution to this challenge by decomposing time series into multi-scale components, thereby decoupling global trends from local details.

Thanks to the effectiveness of the time-frequency analysis, the proposed WTFTP+ framework inherits the core concept of the WTFTP framework, i.e., generating optimal wavelet coefficients to achieve the FTP. Based on the mentioned limitations in WTFTP, the resulting improvements lie in that the WTFTP+ framework directly generates wavelet coefficients of predicted multiple horizons, while WTFTP only performs single-horizon predictions and achieves the multi-horizon prediction in an iterative manner. To this end, an improved Transformer-style encoder-decoder neural architecture is designed to build the FTP model, primarily including four key modules: a trajectory encoder, a wavelet component prompt, a scale-aware wavelet components decoder (SAWCD), and multiple prediction heads. As illustrated in Fig. 6, the overall prediction paradigm is described as follows.

Let P_{N-M:N-1} ∈ R^{6×M} be a trajectory sequence observed over the last M timestamps. The trajectory encoder is designed to project the trajectory sequence into high-dimensional trajectory embeddings TE ∈ R^{d×M}:

TE = TrajectoryEncoder(P_{N-M:N-1}) (6)

where d represents the dimension of trajectory embeddings.

The objective of the SAWCD is to generate multi-scale wavelet components that imply the time-frequency features of predicted horizons. Specifically, the initial wavelet embedding (IWE) is firstly constructed by wavelet component prompt to serve as the input to the SAWCD, including initial low-frequency embedding (IL) and initial high-frequency embedding (IH). Since tail vector of trajectory (defined in this study as the trajectory attributes at the last historical timestep minus that at the previous timestep) is approximately aligned with the trajectory transition trend, it is utilized to construct the prompt of the low-frequency flight pattern, i.e., IL. Considering that it is hard to infer the local motions of predicted horizons from the past horizons, a couple of learnable parameters are trained from historical data to represent high-frequency wavelet embeddings, i.e., IH.

As shown in Fig. 6b, the IWE and TE are fed to the SAWCD to obtain optimal wavelet components (OWC), in which the CDA is introduced to fuse historical temporal features into multi-scale flight patterns, and time-frequency bridging mechanism is designed to promote inter-scale inherent correlating. It can be described as follows:

OWC = SAWCD(IWE, TE) (7)

The SAWCD is implemented by two parallel branches.
• Main branch: follows a Transformer-style architecture, where cross-domain interactions are performed under the assumption that time-domain trajectories lie in the approximate space at a certain scale and multi-scale features are distributed within its subspaces.
• Bypass branch: serves as a time-frequency bridging bypass: wavelet-domain features are first transformed into the time domain via the W2T block, then a self-attention mechanism is designed to capture intrinsic relationships within the time-domain sequences and build the correlations among multi-scale features. The processed features are transformed back into wavelet components through the T2W block to support subsequent time-frequency interactions.

In this work, the dual-branch of the SAWCD focuses on effectively capturing flight transition patterns from both the time and wavelet domains while preserving the orthogonality of wavelet components to facilitate accurate trajectory prediction.

To obtain the multi-horizon trajectory, a set of prediction heads are designed to project the corresponding scale of time-frequency representations into wavelet components. During the prediction procedure, a differential prediction strategy is utilized to avoid unnecessary prediction of the direct-current component, and the inverse discrete wavelet transformation of OWC is applied to obtain the differential sequence of predicted horizons. Finally, an inversely difference operation is employed to obtain trajectory attributes of the next K horizons. The prediction process can be described as:

^P_{N:N+K-1} = IDIFF(IDWT(OWC)) (8)

where IDWT(⋅) is the inverse discrete wavelet transform operation, and IDIFF(⋅) represents the inversely difference operation.

Note that the goal of the WTFTP+ framework is to predict the wavelet coefficients of the future trajectory sequence by considering the time-frequency features of the observations. During the training process, the mean squared error (MSE) loss is used to quantify the difference between the predicted and actual wavelet coefficients, thereby driving the optimization of the neural network parameters. The implementation details of each module are described in the following sections.

Trajectory encoder
The trajectory encoder is constructed by trajectory point embedding block and Transformer encoder blocks, which aims to extract the spatial-temporal dependencies of the observations. Specifically, to better learn the latent features from the observations, it is essential to map the trajectory points to high-dimensional embedding space to extract discriminative spatial features. Similar to the WTFTP framework, a simple yet effective trajectory point embedding block is employed to project the trajectory point into embedding space, which can be described as:

I = σ(P_{N-M:N-1} * W_{i1} + b_{i1}) * W_{i2} + b_{i2} (9)

where P_{N-M:N-1} ∈ R^{M×6} represents the observed trajectory sequence. W_{i1} ∈ R^{6×D//2}, and W_{i2} ∈ R^{D//2×D} are learnable transformation matrices. b_{i1} ∈ R^{D//2} and b_{i2} ∈ R^D are bias vectors. σ(⋅) represents the ReLU activation function. M is the number of observed trajectory points, and D is the feature space dimension. // denotes the floor division operator.

The WTFTP+ framework employs the Transformer encoder33 to extract the temporal dependencies among observed trajectory points. Since the self-attention mechanism is permutation-invariant, a positional encoding (PE) strategy is designed to establish the relative positional relationships of trajectory sequence. Therefore, the observed trajectory embeddings TE can be obtained as follows:

TE = TransformerEncoder(PE(I)) (10)

where TransformerEncoder(⋅) is multi-layer Transformer encoder. PE(⋅) applies sine and cosine functions to generate positional embeddings with dimension of D and add them into I.

Scale-aware wavelet component decoder
The SAWCD is stacked by several ITD layers, which incorporates time-frequency analysis capabilities by the proposed CDA and time-frequency bridging mechanism. Specifically, the initial wavelet embedding IWE is constructed to serve as the input of the SAWCD, which is further sequentially fed to the ITD layers into generate multi-scale wavelet component representations. As shown in Fig. 6b, the core architecture of the ITD layer follows the standard Transformer decoder layer with the following improvements:
• The scale-aware mechanism is incorporated into the self-attention and feed-forward network to preserve the orthogonality of inter-scale features, allowing the model to learn single-scale flight transition pattern during the training procedure.
• Since the multi-scale features are distributed in mutually orthogonal subspaces of the observed trajectory approximation space, the CDA is designed to incorporate embeddings of the observed trajectory sequence into the multi-scale features.
• Most importantly, a time-frequency bridging mechanism is proposed to extract inherent time-frequency correlations among multi-scale features while maintaining their orthogonality, which serves as the bridging bypass in the decoder.

Initial wavelet embedding. The initial wavelet embedding consists of two stacked parts: the initial low-frequency (IL) embeddings and the initial high-frequency (IH) embeddings. These embeddings are arranged in a descending order of time resolution, and the embeddings of the same resolution are sequentially grouped as illustrated in Supplementary Fig. 1. In general, low-frequency wavelet components represent the global trend of the trajectory sequence, while the high-frequency wavelet components imply the local motion details. In this work, the low-frequency flight pattern is transformed into a high-dimensional vector and replicated to generate the IL ∈ R^{t_L×D}, as shown below:

IL = REP(σ((P_{N-1} - P_{N-2})^T * W_{d1} + b_{d1}) * W_{d2} + b_{d2}, t_L) (11)

where W_{d1} ∈ R^{D×D//2} and W_{d2} ∈ R^{D//2×D} are learnable weight matrices. b_{d1} ∈ R^{D//2} and b_{d2} ∈ R^D are learnable bias vectors. t_L is the sequence length of low-frequency wavelet component in level-L wavelet analysis. The operation REP(a, b) replicate the vector a along the column dimension for b times.

For initial high-frequency components, considering the complicated predictability of future local motions under incomplete maneuvering intentions, a couple of learnable parameters are employed to model the distribution of fast dynamics from historical data. In addition, considering the orthogonality of inter-scale wavelet components, a learnable scale encoding (SE) strategy is proposed to enhance the scale discriminability of the initial embeddings. The PE strategy is also applied to enhance sequential discriminability along the temporal dimension. Mathematically, the initial wavelet embedding can be obtained by:

IWE = PE(Σ_{i=1}^L {IH_{i} [t_i : t_i, :]} + SE[j, :], IL + SE[j+1, :]) (12)

where IWE ∈ R^{t_A×D} serves as the input of the SAWCD, which corresponds to the wavelet components of the future flight trajectory. IH ∈ R^{(t_A-t_L)×D} is the learnable IH embedding. SE ∈ R^{(L+1)×D} is the learnable scale embedding. L is the level of wavelet analysis. {t_i}_{i∈[1,L]∩Z} stands for the sequence length of level-i wavelet component, while t_A = t_L + Σ_{i=1}^L t_i stands for that of stacked wavelet components in L levels of wavelet analysis. {t_i}_{i∈[1,L]∩Z} can be calculated below:

t_i = {H, i=0; ⌊t_{i-1}/2⌋+l, i=1, ..., L} (13)

where H is the predicted steps.

Scale-aware self-attention. To investigate sequential dependency of intra-scale flight patterns, in each ITD layer, the self-attention mechanism is applied to obtain enhanced wavelet embedding (EWE) derived from IWE. Therefore, a scale-aware self-attention (SA2) mechanism is designed to preserve temporal causality and prevent inter-scale feature leakage by employing a well-crafted mask matrix. The residual connection, followed by layer normalization (LN), is utilized to retain the learned semantics during the information propagation process. The inference process can be described as follows:

EWE = LN(SA2(IWE) + IWE) (14)

where EWE ∈ R^{t_A×D} is the enhanced wavelet embeddings. The attention weight W ∈ R^{t_A×t_A} is calculated by:

W = Softmax(Q * K^T / √{D/m} + Mask_{sa2}) (15)

Mask_{sa2}[i, j] = {0, i∈[t_A-t_L, t_A]∩Z, j∈[t_A-t_L, i]∩Z; -1, otherwise} (16)

where Q, K ∈ R^{t_A×(D/m)} are the query and key features of IWE. m is the number of heads. Mask_{sa2} ∈ R^{t_A×t_A} is the mask matrix.

Cross-domain attention. To learn the underlying flight transition patterns of the observation sequence, a CDA mechanism is utilized to incorporate the prior transition patterns from observed trajectory representation into enhanced wavelet embeddings. Since multi-scale features are generally distributed in the subspace of the time-domain approximation space, the CDA is expected to perform feature interaction between the trajectory encoder and the SAWCD, which learn wavelet-domain flight pattern from observed trajectory. Specifically, attention weights are obtained using: EWE serves as the queries, and the observed trajectory representation TE serves as both keys and values, as shown below:

FWE = LN(CDA(EWE, TE) + EWE) (17)

where FWE ∈ R^{t_A×D} is the output, i.e., fused wavelet embedding. Similarly, the residual connection, followed by LN, is utilized to retain semantics during the information propagation process.

Time-frequency bridging. Although the CDA effectively extracts informative flight transition patterns from the observed trajectory, due to the orthogonality of these wavelet components, it is still hard to capture inherent dependency between global trend and local motion patterns. In this work, a time-frequency bridging mechanism is proposed to extract the intrinsic correlations across multi-scale wavelet components to preserve the wavelet orthogonality, which is expected to fully leverage the time-frequency analysis capability of wavelet transform in the FTP task. Note that time-frequency bridging mechanism is performed in parallel with the CDA procedure as a bypass operation on EWE, which achieves an effective and efficient feature learning. Specifically, the bridging bypass first transforms multi-scale components of enhanced wavelet embeddings into a unified time domain by a trainable W2T block. Then time-domain self-attention is designed to establish the interaction bridge for inter-scale features and capture significant dependency among multi-scale flight patterns. To facilitate subsequent procedure, a trainable T2W block is proposed to regain time-frequency representations to support the whole time-frequency analysis for the FTP task.

Let low- and high-frequency features in wavelet analysis at the i-th level be Lo_i, Hi_i ∈ R^{t_i×D}, respectively. Taking L=3 levels of wavelet analysis as an example, the time-frequency bridging process is illustrated in Supplementary Fig. 5 by cascading W2T block, time-domain self-attention, and T2W block. The W2T procedure can be described as follows:

Lo_{i-1} = σ(ALT(Lo_i, Hi_i)^T * W_{lw2t} + b_{lw2t})^T, i=1,2,...,L (18)

Lo_L = EWE[t_A-t_L : t_A, :] (19)

Hi_i = EWE[t_A-t_L-t_i : t_A-t_L, :], i=1,2,...,L (20)

where W_{lw2t} ∈ R^{2t_i×t_{i-1}} is learnable inverse wavelet transform matrix at the i-th level of the W2T procedure, and b_{lw2t} ∈ R^{t_{i-1}} serves as learnable bias. ALT(Lo, Hi) alternate the rows of Lo and Hi along the time dimension. Notably, the learnable inverse wavelet transform matrix consists of: i) a sparse matrix constructed from wavelet filter parameters (as described in Supplementary Information, Section “The wavelet-to-time domain procedure”), and ii) learnable parameters to pad the sparse elements in i). Thus, the W2T procedure is able to achieve the inverse wavelet transform-like operations, in which the design of the learnable parameters facilitates adaptive adjustment of the bridging bypass and promotes the interaction of inter-scale features.

Through iterative process of Eq. (18), low- and high-frequency features at the same level are jointly reconstructed into the lower-frequency. As the level i decreases in the W2T procedure, the time resolution of Lo_i goes higher, which are ultimately transformed into Lo_0 in time domain. Then, the self-attention mechanism is employed to perform feature interactions by extracting inherent correlations within Lo_0, as shown below:

^Lo_0 = LN(TSA(Lo_0) + Lo_0) (21)

where ^Lo_0 represents the output time-domain features. TSA(⋅) represents time-domain self-attention. In addition, the residual connection followed by LN is utilized to retain semantics during information propagation.

As an inverse operation, the T2W procedure aims to regain time-frequency representations to facilitate subsequent inference, which in practice transforms ^Lo_0 into multi-scale wavelet features, as shown below:

^Lo_i = LN(σ(^Lo_{i-1}^T * W_{lt2wl} + b_{lt2wl})^T + Lo_i), i=1,2,...,L (22)

^Hi_i = LN(σ(^Lo_{i-1}^T * W_{lt2wh} + b_{lt2wh})^T + Hi_i), i=1,2,...,L (23)

BWE = {^Hi_i, ^Lo_L}_{i∈[1,L]∩Z} (24)

where ^Lo_i, ^Hi_i ∈ R^{t_i×D} represent low- and high-frequency features in T2W procedure at the i-th level. W_{lt2wl}, W_{lt2wh} ∈ R^{t_{i-1}×t_i} are learnable low- and high-frequency wavelet transform matrices at the i-th level of the T2W procedure, and b_{lt2wl}, b_{lt2wh} ∈ R^{t_i} serve as learnable low- and high-frequency bias vectors. The learnable low- and high-frequency wavelet transform matrices are constructed in the similar way with the learnable inverse wavelet transform matrices (as described in Supplementary Information, Section “The time-to-wavelet domain procedure”), and also consist of two parts, the wavelet filter parameters and the learnable parameters. After the time-frequency bridging, ^Lo_L serves as the low-frequency component, while {^Hi_i}_{i∈[1,L]∩Z} serve as the multi-scale high-frequency components. Finally, the bridged wavelet embeddings BWE ∈ R^{t_A×D} is obtained by concatenating the ^Lo_L and {^Hi_i}_{i∈[1,L]∩Z}. The T2W procedure is the inverse process of the W2T procedure. As the level i increases, the time-domain feature ^Lo_0 is decomposed back into wavelet domain with frequency resolution gradually going higher.

Scale-aware feed-forward network. In each ITD layer, the FWE and BWE are aggregated and further extracted in the scale-aware feed-forward networks (SAFFNs) by a shared architectures with unique parameters, preserving the orthogonality of inter-scale features and yielding complete wavelet embeddings CWE ∈ R^{t_A×D}. The SAFFN can be expressed as:

CWE = [^Q_L, ^Q_{L-1}, ..., ^Q_0] (25)

^Q_L = LN(SAFFN(Σ_{i=1}^L MWE[t_i, :]) + Σ_{i=1}^L MWE[t_i, :]) (26)

^Q_{L-j} = LN(SAFFN(Σ_{i=1}^L MWE[t_i : t_{L-j+1} + t_i, :]) + Σ_{i=1}^L MWE[t_i : t_{L-j+1} + t_i, :]), j=1,2,...,L (27)

MWE = FWE + BWE (28)

where MWE ∈ R^{t_A×D} is the sum of FWE and BWE. ^Q_L ∈ R^{t_L×D} is the low-frequency components of the CWE, while {^Q_i}_{i∈[1,L]∩Z} ∈ R^{t_{L-i+1}×D} are the multi-scale high-frequency components. {SAFFN(⋅)}_{i∈[1,L]∩Z} represents the scale-aware feedforward network for Hi, while SAFFN(⋅) for Lo_L. Similarly, the residual connection followed by LN is also utilized to retain semantics during information propagation.

Prediction and post-processing
Due to the multi-scale and orthogonality properties of wavelet components, multiple prediction heads are required to map complete wavelet embeddings of the last ITD layer to obtain wavelet components of certain predicted horizons. Each prediction head is implemented by multi-layer perceptrons (MLP) (i.e., two linear layers with an ReLU activation function). The prediction process can be described as follows:

^Q_i = PredictionHead_i(Q), i=0,1,2,...,L (29)

where {PredictionHead_i(⋅)}_{i∈[1,L]∩Z} represents the i-th prediction head for generating ^Q_i, i.e., the desired WTC according to definition of wavelet component in our previous work22.

Subsequently, to achieve the FTP task with trajectory attributes of predicted horizons, the IDWT operation is applied to transform predicted wavelet components back to the time domain, further reconstructing the predicted future trajectory sequence, as in our previous work22. Mathematically, the prediction for the j-th attribute ^P'_{N:N+H-1}[j-1, :] is shown as:

^P'_{N:N+H-1}[j-1, :] = IDIFF(TRIM(IDWT({^Q_i[j-1, :]}_{i∈[0,L]∩Z}))), j=1,2,...,6 (30)

where TRIM(⋅) is applied to crop out the redundant segments at the end of the trajectory sequence due to the signal extension, i.e., the first H elements along the time dimension retained. IDIFF(⋅) represents the inversely difference operation to avoid unnecessary prediction for the direct-current component.

Loss function
To facilitate the learning of multi-scale flight patterns, the MSE loss function performed on wavelet components is proposed to update the learnable parameters of the WTFTP+ framework, following the similar strategy to the WTFTP framework. Furthermore, an L2 regularization penalty is applied to optimize the learnable parameters within the W2T and T2W transform matrices. This regularization constrains the deviation from the standard wavelet filters, thereby preserving the effectiveness of the time-frequency bridging process. The loss function is formulated as follows:

L = (epoch/total_epoch) * (L_{w2t} + L_{t2w}) + L_{wavelet} (31)

where L_{w2t}, L_{t2w} are one part of the loss function and the L2 regularization for the W2T and T2W transform matrices, respectively. epoch and total_epoch are the current and total epochs during the training procedure, whereby a proper ratio allows the learnable parameters to have a broader optimization exploration space in the early stages of training, while gradually converging toward the wavelet filter as training progresses. The details of L_{w2t}, L_{t2w} are described as follows:

L_{w2t} = β * Σ_{i=1}^l Σ_{j=1}^L (||W_{w2t, i,j}||_F^2 + ||b_{w2t, i,j}||_2^2) (32)

L_{t2w} = β * Σ_{i=1}^l Σ_{j=1}^L (||W_{t2w, i,j}||_F^2 + ||W_{t2w, i,j}||_F^2 + ||b_{t2w, i,j}||_2^2 + ||b_{t2w, i,j}||_2^2) (33)

where β is the weight for both of the L2 regularizations. L is the level of wavelet analysis. l is the number of decoder layers. W_{w2t, i,j}, b_{w2t, i,j} are the W2T transform matrix and bias vector at the j-th level of wavelet analysis in the i-th layer of the ITD. W_{t2w, i,j}, b_{t2w, i,j} are the T2W transform matrix and bias vector at the j-th level of wavelet analysis in the i-th layer of the ITD for the low-frequency, while W_{t2w, i,j}, b_{t2w, i,j} for the high-frequency. ||⋅|| is the Euclidean norm. Since the spectral norm is difficult to calculate for transform matrices in time-frequency bridging, the Frobenius norm, ||⋅||_F, is utilized to optimize the upper bound of the spectral norm. The MSE loss of the wavelet component, i.e., L_{wavelet}, is calculated by:

L_{wavelet} = 1/(L-k) * d * Σ_{i=1}^{L-k} Σ_{j=1}^d (c_{i,j}^k - ^c_{i,j}^k)^2 (34)

where h_{L-k} is the length of WTC_k 22, satisfying h_{L-k} = t_{L-k+1} except h_L = t_L. d=6 is the number of trajectory attributes. ^c_{i,j}^k is the value of the i-th predicted wavelet coefficient in the j-th attribute of WTC after applying the DWT operation to the future trajectory differential sequence, while c_{i,j}^k is the ground truth.

### Reviewer 3

The paper under review proposes a wavelet-based method for an efficient flight trajectory prediction in the multi-horizon
setting. The work appears promising, as it employs frequency-domain analysis in the flight trajectory prediction task, in
contrast to data-driven methods. The proposed method can be viewed as an extension of the existing Wavelet Transform-
based Flight Trajectory Prediction (WTFTP) framework to circumvent its limitations, in that WTFTP suffers from a
performance bottleneck in multi-horizon prediction due to its inherent single-horizon inference paradigm. This novel
framework (WTFTP+) is implemented with a generalized encoder-decoder architecture, in which the encoder is employed to
extract the abstract features from the observed trajectory sequence, while the decoder is applied to generate the optimal
wavelet coefficients for the predicted horizons. In order to maintain orthogonality of the multi-scale wavelet components, in
the decoder, the orthogonal wavelet components are first bridged into the time domain for promotive interaction, and
subsequently bridged back into the wavelet-transformed domain to obtain enhanced features of inherent flight patterns. The
validity of the WTFTP+ method is demonstrated via several experiments on a real-world flight trajectory dataset, whereas
some baseline comparisons are incorporated into the experimental analysis to provide a comprehensive evaluation of the
method.
In conclusion, I find the paper very well-written and the results quite interesting from an empirical perspective. Though a
reasonable discussion on the theoretical underpinnings of the method can be found in the paper, an extensive theoretical
performance analysis of the WTFTP+ method is not provided. Moreover, the choice of wavelet function, decomposition
levels, and LSTM hyperparameters may significantly impact results. In this regard, a more systematic sensitivity analysis
would be beneficial. Since the model performs well on U.S. flight data, it is unclear how well it would generalise to other
airspaces or data sources without retraining. Overall, the WTFTP+ method is somewhat more explainable in contrast to the
data-driven frameworks.

3. Multi-resolution analysis (Pages 2-4, Section 3, Supplementary Information)
Multi-resolution analysis (MRA) theory [1], also known as multi-scale analysis, provides a
coarse-to-fine feature representation of signals while simplifying complex integration
calculations, as the essence of discrete wavelet transforms. In MRA, signals undergo a series
of filtering and downsampling operations to yield feature sequences with physical significance
at different scales. The general procedure of MRA involves decomposing a signal into two
fundamental components: low-frequency subbands and high-frequency subbands. The former,
obtained through low-pass filtering, constitutes the approximation coefficients; the latter,
generated by high-pass filtering, represents the detail coefficients. To achieve finer frequency
resolution, the low-frequency subbands undergo further decomposition. As decomposition
levels progress, MRA delivers multi-scale time-frequency representations of the signal.

In practice, with the signal projection onto the approximation space at scale j, it can be

In the flight process, the overall motion trends of the aircraft are typically determined by
historical transition patterns, flight plans, and real-time ATC instructions. To be specific, for a
certain route shown in Supplementary Fig. 3, the trajectory always evolves toward the
designated waypoint (in the flight plans), indicating that the planned route can imply the overall
flight trend. At the same time, local variations are introduced by weather conditions, aircraft
performance parameters, and pilot-specific operations. In other words, a flight trajectory can be
regarded as a combination of global trends and local details. While different flights in similar
scenarios may follow similar overall trends, their local motion details often vary significantly,
which limits the prediction accuracy of the conventional FTP approaches.
The wavelet transform provides an intuitive solution to this challenge by decomposing time
series into multiscale components, thereby decoupling local details from global trends. This
time–frequency analysis forms the theoretical foundation of both WTFTP and WTFTP+.
Orthogonal wavelets with compact support facilitate the identification of maneuvers such as
turns, climbs, or descents at different scales. Moreover, local motion details can influence global
patterns, implying inherent dependencies across multi-scale wavelet components. WTFTP+
builds upon this foundation by introducing scale-aware wavelet component decoder and time–
frequency bridging mechanisms, which enable effective interaction among multi-scale wavelet
components without breaking orthogonality. These technical improvements allow the model to
jointly capture global motion trends and fine-grained local dynamics, thereby addressing
performance bottlenecks inherent in conventional FTP approaches.

patterns.

Multi-resolution analysis (MRA) theory [1], also known as multi-scale analysis, provides a

7.3. Wavelet functions and decomposition levels (Pages 9-11, Supplementary Information)
In this section, the impacts of different wavelet basis functions and decomposition levels are
investigated to validate the effectiveness of the selected Haar wavelet basis function.
Specifically, the Symlets (sym2) and Coiflets (coif1) are selected as alternatives to the Haar
wavelet used in the original WTFTP+ framework. As shown in Supplementary Table 5, the
WTFTP+ framework still achieves the desired FTP performance even with other wavelet basis
functions, which demonstrates the robustness of the proposed WTFTP+ framework. However,
the performance exhibited a slight degradation when the WTFTP+ was implemented with
Symlets and Coiflets functions. Considering that the predicted trajectory length is shorter than
that of common time series, the wavelet basis with a relatively short length of compact support
suffices to achieve short-term prediction. The Haar wavelet, as the simplest basis function with
a length of support being only 1, enables superior sensitivity in capturing abrupt changes and
local discontinuities in trajectory data. In contrast, despite Symlets with 2 orders and Coiflets
with 1 order offering smoother frequency responses, their extended support means a single
wavelet coefficient may incorporate information from multiple time points, making it impossible
to pinpoint the exact instant at which a maneuver occurred. This “tail effect” or “temporal
ambiguity” weakens the significance of local critical information in short-term forecasts, thereby
degrading prediction performance. Heisenberg's uncertainty principle dictates that a signal
cannot achieve arbitrarily high resolution simultaneously in both the time domain and the
frequency domain. Frequency resolution can be enhanced through multi-level wavelet analysis.
Therefore, when selecting a wavelet basis, greater emphasis should be placed on temporal
locality in short-term forecasts. The tightly supported Haar wavelet with the shortest support
emerges as the optimal choice within the WTFTP+ framework, leading to superior prediction
performance.
7.2. Hyperparameters (Pages 9-10, Supplementary Information)
This section presents ablation studies on the hyperparameters of the WTFTP+ framework,
which mainly focus on the dimension of trajectory embeddings and the number of Transformer
layers in the trajectory encoder and the SAWCD module.
For trajectory embeddings, in addition to the original configuration of 128 dimensions,
experiments are conducted with 64 and 256 dimensions. As shown in Supplementary Table 3,
the results indicate that 128 dimensions provide the best balance between representation
capability and computational efficiency. It is believed that the proposed model (with 64-
dimensional embedding) is insufficient to capture the complex spatial–temporal patterns of
flight trajectories, which finally results in under-representation and degraded prediction
accuracy. Conversely, increasing the dimension to 256 might introduce redundant features that
do not substantially improve predictive performance while significantly increasing the
computational efficiency of the model. The above experimental results suggest that 128
dimensions are the most suitable selection to extract trajectory representations in the WTFTP+
framework.
For the number of Transformer layers, we further evaluate two additional configurations beyond
the original setting (4 stacked Transformer layers in Trajectory encoder and 2 stacked
Transformer layers for SAWCD): (i) 2 stacked Transformer layers in Trajectory encoder and 1
Transformer layer for SAWCD, and (ii) 4 stacked Transformer layers in Trajectory encoder and
4 stacked Transformer layers for SAWCD. Experimental results reveal the following two
important insights: first, reducing the depth of the model slightly (i.e., setting (i)) leads to
degraded performance, likely due to overfitting and the disruption of the balance between
feature abstraction and interaction depth. Second, further improving the depth of the model to
setting (ii) obtains comparable performance to the original configuration, which indicates deeper
layers can maintain but not substantially enhance the model accuracy.
Overall, these results demonstrate that the adopted hyperparameter settings represent a
rational and empirically validated design choice for the WTFTP+ framework.

Response to Reviewer #4
The paper proposes an enhanced flight trajectory prediction framework (WTFTP+) that
leverages time-frequency wavelet transforms and a direct multi-horizon prediction paradigm.
This model builds upon the authors' earlier work by introducing a time-frequency bridging
mechanism designed to enable inter-scale feature interaction without violating wavelet
component orthogonality.
Overall, the approach is well-explained and supported by comprehensive experimentation.
However, I have the following major and minor comments:
Major Comment：
Comment #1: While the incorporation of wavelet transforms into trajectory prediction is
interesting, the core contribution appears incremental. The WTFTP+ framework primarily
refines existing idea, such as direct multi-horizon prediction and inter-scale attention, rather
than offering fundamentally new algorithmic or theoretical insights. As such, the contributions
fall short of the novelty and depth typically expected for a journal publication.
Author response: Thanks for your insightful comments, which help us to better clarify the
novelty and contributions of our work.
Although the WTFTP+ framework retains the core idea (time-frequency modelling) from, it
addresses several fundamental limitations that have not been effectively solved by existing FTP
approaches, including both time-domain and frequency-domain methods.
In the original WTFTP, multi-horizon predictions were obtained through an iterative paradigm,
which inevitably leads to error accumulation, especially for high-frequency wavelet components
to capture local motion details. Moreover, the independent decoding of each wavelet scale,
based on the strict mathematical orthogonality assumption, with limited considerations on the
inherent inter-scale dependencies that usually occur in real flight scenarios.
The proposed WTFTP+ introduces three key innovations to overcome these bottlenecks:
1. Direct multi-horizon prediction paradigm: WTFTP+ replaces the iterative strategy with
a generalized direct-prediction encoder–decoder framework. This significantly mitigates
cumulative errors over extended horizons and enables more reliable performance in real-
world ATC operations where long-term forecasts are critical. In addition, compared to the
WTFTP framework, a Transformer-style architecture is designed to implement the neural
network of the WTFTP+, which enables more effective sequential modeling for multi-
horizon FTP tasks.
2. Scale-aware wavelet component decoder (SAWCD): Instead of separate decoders for
each scale, SAWCD integrates the learning process to simultaneously model intra-scale
flight patterns and capture inter-scale correlations,while preserving the orthogonality.
3. Time–frequency bridging mechanism: To enhance inherent dependencies within flight
patterns across different time-frequency scales and retain orthogonality and enable inter-
scale interaction, WTFTP+ proposes a bidirectional bridging between wavelet and time
domains via learnable W2T and T2W procedures. This mechanism allows the model to
exploit intrinsic dependencies that are invisible when each wavelet scale is treated in
isolation.
Extensive experiments and ablation studies confirm that WTFTP+ achieves substantial and
consistent performance improvements over both the original WTFTP and competitive baselines,
with up to 40% relative reduction in mean deviation error at the 5-minute horizon. Meanwhile,
WTFTP+ not only addresses the key limitation of WTFTP in long-horizon prediction, but also
provides the flexibility to incorporate ATC instructions, thereby enhancing its ability to model
instruction-driven maneuvers. Furthermore, in this revision, additional experiments on a new
dataset (U.S. airspace) further verify the strong generalization capability of the proposed
framework.
By jointly tackling error accumulation and cross-scale dependency modeling, i.e., two key
issues in existing time–frequency FTP research. WTFTP+ expands the applicability of wavelet-
based methods from single-horizon, component-wise prediction to robust multi-horizon
forecasting in operationally complex ATC environments. Therefore, it is believed that the
contributions of WTFTP+ are not incremental refinements, but rather represent a meaningful
step toward integrating time–frequency analysis with modern sequence modeling for the flight
trajectory prediction task.
